Atlas's 2023 10-K discloses Texas operations as a material portion of production; TRC's regulatory changes directly affect Atlas's operating costs and reserve development.

portalBindings.relationshipNote: FCC regulates tower siting, antenna placement, and RF exposure under 47 CFR §17 and 47 CFR §1.1307. AMT must comply with FCC environmental assessments (NEPA) and RF-hazard rules for all 225K+ sites. FCC's 2023 tower-siting streamlining rule (47 CFR §1.6100) accelerated small-cell permitting; AMT benefits from faster deployment cycles. FCC's spectrum auctions (C-band, mmWave) drive tenant capex and incremental revenue. Ongoing FCC monitoring of tower-siting delays and permitting backlogs in dense urban markets.

FAA regulates tower lighting, marking, and airspace clearance under 14 CFR Part 77 and FAA Order 7460.1. AMT must maintain lighting systems and file airspace notifications for all 225K+ sites. FAA's 2024 rule on unlit-tower exemptions (14 CFR §77.9) reduced lighting costs for non-critical sites; AMT estimates $10-15M annual savings. FAA's drone-airspace integration rules (Part 107) create new compliance requirements for tower-mounted sensors. Ongoing FAA coordination on tower-siting in proximity to airports.

IRS regulates AMT's REIT status under IRC §856-860. AMT must maintain 90% dividend payout ratio, <5% related-party revenue, and <10% taxable REIT subsidiary (TRS) income. IRS audits REIT compliance annually; AMT's last audit (2021) resulted in no material adjustments. IRS's 2024 guidance on carried-interest rules and TRS income limits creates compliance complexity. AMT's dividend payout ratio 91% (compliant); TRS income (CoreSite) <8% of total. Ongoing IRS monitoring of REIT tax-law changes and dividend-payout-ratio sustainability.

portalBindings.entityName: Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario (AGCO)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: AGCO regulates gaming in Ontario, Canada. Caesars operates gaming properties in Ontario (e.g., Caesars Windsor); AGCO oversees gaming licenses, compliance, and operational standards. Caesars' Canadian operations represent. AGCO regulatory requirements include gaming machine approvals, player protection programs, and AML/BSA compliance. Regulatory risk is lower in Canada vs. US due to stable regulatory environment; however, AGCO can impose operational restrictions or license suspension for compliance failures.

SEC oversees EL's public company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings), insider trading compliance, and proxy statements (DEF14A). EL's activist investor exposure (Pengxin Capital, others) triggers heightened SEC scrutiny of board independence and executive compensation. Recent SEC focus on climate and ESG disclosures (proposed rules 2023–2024) requires EL to expand sustainability reporting in 10-K Item 1A risk factors and MD&A. EL's debt refinancing activities and credit facility amendments require SEC Form 8-K disclosure.

FTC enforces truth-in-advertising standards for EL's beauty claims (skincare efficacy, anti-aging, sustainability). EL's 2023 sustainability claims ("clean beauty," "eco-friendly packaging") face FTC scrutiny under Guides Against Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260); FTC issued warning letters to beauty companies (2023) on unsubstantiated environmental claims. EL's influencer partnerships and social media marketing (Instagram, TikTok) require FTC compliance on disclosure of material connections (#ad, #sponsored). FTC's ongoing investigation into beauty industry pricing practices (2023–2024) may impact EL's pricing power.

SEC regulates Live Nation's public company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings). Live Nation files quarterly and annual reports disclosing financial performance, risk factors, and material events. SEC enforcement actions on disclosure accuracy are low-probability but high-impact. Live Nation's Ticketmaster subsidiary is subject to SEC scrutiny on revenue recognition and take-rate disclosure. Recent SEC focus on dynamic pricing disclosure may require enhanced transparency on Ticketmaster's pricing algorithms.

DOJ is investigating Live Nation's Ticketmaster subsidiary for antitrust violations related to bundling practices (forcing venues to use Ticketmaster for ticketing as condition of Live Nation touring promotion). Investigation began 2022; settlement negotiations ongoing (2024). Potential remedies include forced interoperability, divestiture of Ticketmaster, or bundling restrictions. Settlement terms could reduce Ticketmaster's take-rate revenue by estimated 10–20% and force platform interoperability. High-impact regulatory risk; settlement timeline uncertain.

FTC has authority over Live Nation's consumer protection practices, including Ticketmaster's dynamic pricing, fee disclosure, and bundling practices. FTC has issued guidance on dynamic pricing transparency and unfair practices. FTC enforcement actions against Ticketmaster are possible if dynamic pricing is deemed deceptive or unfair. Potential remedies include fee disclosure requirements, price transparency mandates, or consumer refund obligations. Regulatory risk is moderate; FTC coordination with DOJ antitrust division increases enforcement likelihood.

EU, UK, and Australian regulators are investigating Live Nation's international touring and ticketing practices. EU competition authorities are examining Ticketmaster's market dominance in European ticketing. UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has opened investigation into Ticketmaster's bundling practices. Australian ACCC is investigating dynamic pricing and fee transparency. International regulatory actions could force Ticketmaster to modify pricing or bundling practices in key markets (Europe, UK, Australia), reducing international revenue by estimated 5–15%.

SEC oversees Roku's 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K filings; enforces Sarbanes-Oxley compliance. Roku's CIK 0001428439 filed 2024 10-K on 2024-02-29. SEC scrutiny on ad-tech consolidation (e.g., Roku's 35% CTV share) may trigger merger-review thresholds if Roku pursues acquisitions. Roku's stock-based compensation disclosures subject to SEC scrutiny.

FTC monitors Roku's market concentration in CTV ad-tech (35% share) and potential antitrust concerns. FTC's 2023 scrutiny of ad-tech consolidation (e.g., Broadcom/Qualcomm) signals heightened enforcement. Roku's data-privacy practices (first-party data collection) subject to FTC enforcement under Section 5 (unfair/deceptive practices). No active FTC matter disclosed as of Q3 2024.

EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) and GDPR regulate Roku's data practices and market conduct in Europe. Roku's 2024 European expansion (platform revenue growth in EU) subject to DMA compliance. GDPR fines up to 4% of global revenue create material compliance cost. Roku's 10-K discloses EU regulatory risk as material to international growth strategy.

FCC regulates Roku TV hardware (RF emissions, spectrum compliance) and content moderation on Roku Channel. FCC's 2024 net-neutrality enforcement may impact Roku's content delivery and ISP relationships. Roku's Roku Channel (free ad-supported streaming service) subject to FCC content-moderation standards. No active FCC enforcement matter disclosed.

The SEC oversees Squarespace's financial reporting and disclosure obligations as a public company (NASDAQ: SQSP). Squarespace files 10-K (annual), 10-Q (quarterly), 8-K (event-driven), and DEF14A (proxy) filings with the SEC. The SEC enforces compliance with Regulation S-X (financial statements) and Regulation S-K (business and risk disclosures). Squarespace has no material SEC enforcement actions or investigations as of 2024. Relationship is regulatory and ongoing; filings are available on EDGAR (CIK 0001496963).

The FTC oversees Squarespace's consumer protection and data privacy practices. Squarespace is subject to FTC Act Section 5 (unfair or deceptive practices) and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (financial data privacy). Squarespace maintains a privacy policy compliant with FTC standards and discloses data-handling practices. The FTC has no material enforcement actions against Squarespace as of 2024. Relationship is regulatory and ongoing; Squarespace's privacy policy is publicly available on its website.

The EDPB oversees compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which regulates Squarespace's handling of EU residents' personal data. Squarespace is subject to GDPR requirements for data processing, consent, and data-subject rights. Squarespace maintains a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) with customers and discloses GDPR compliance in its privacy policy. Squarespace has no material GDPR enforcement actions as of 2024. Relationship is regulatory and ongoing; disclosed in 10-K Item 1A risk factors.

Charter is a major distributor of Disney's premium video content, including ABC, ESPN, Disney Channel, FX, and Hulu programming. As a significant customer, Charter's subscriber base and carriage decisions materially influence Disney's licensing revenue and video segment profitability. Their relationship involves annual rate negotiations and occasional carriage disputes impacting both parties' margins.

SEC oversees Disney's public company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings). Disney's Q3 2024 10-Q filing (filed Nov 2024) disclosed streaming subscriber metrics, Parks attendance, and content impairments. SEC scrutiny on streaming accounting (revenue recognition, content capitalization) and executive compensation (Dodd-Frank say-on-pay votes). Disney's 2024 proxy statement (DEF14A) disclosed CEO compensation ($27M+ total) and board composition. Disclosed in Disney SEC filings and investor relations.

FCC regulates Disney's broadcast television (ABC, ESPN, FX Networks) and satellite operations. FCC scrutiny on sports-rights consolidation (ESPN's exclusive sports contracts); potential antitrust review of Disney's media ownership concentration. FCC's 2023 media ownership rules review examined Disney's broadcast + cable + streaming portfolio. Disney's ABC network holds FCC broadcast licenses (renewed 2020, next renewal 2026). Disclosed in Disney 10-K Item 1A (regulatory risks) and FCC filings.

DOJ Antitrust Division scrutinizes Disney's media M&A activity and market concentration. DOJ's 2023 review of Disney's Fox acquisition (completed 2019, $71.3B) examined competitive impacts on theatrical, streaming, and sports. DOJ monitoring of Disney's ESPN sports-rights consolidation and potential antitrust concerns. DOJ's 2024 antitrust enforcement priorities include media consolidation and streaming market competition. Disclosed in Disney 10-K Item 1A (regulatory risks) and DOJ antitrust filings.

European Commission regulates Disney's European operations (Disneyland Paris, Disney+ in EU markets). EU Digital Services Act (2024) imposes content moderation and algorithmic transparency requirements on Disney+ streaming platform. EU antitrust scrutiny on Disney's media ownership in Europe; potential restrictions on exclusive sports-rights contracts. Disney's European revenue ~$15B annually (25% of total); EU regulatory compliance costs estimated $50–100M annually. Disclosed in Disney 10-K Item 1A (international regulatory risks) and EU filings.

portalBindings.relationshipNote: SEC oversees BAH's public company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, proxy statements). BAH is subject to Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) compliance, audit committee oversight, and quarterly earnings guidance. SEC filings are primary source of BAH financial data and risk disclosures; no material SEC enforcement actions against BAH in past 5 years.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) & Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: FAR and DFARS govern all BAH federal contracts; compliance is critical to contract award and performance. Recent DFARS cybersecurity requirements (CMMC 2.0) and supply-chain risk management (SCRM) create new compliance costs for BAH and its suppliers. BAH invests heavily in FAR/DFARS compliance infrastructure; non-compliance could result in contract suspension.

FTC monitors BAH for antitrust compliance and competitive practices. BAH's market share in federal consulting is significant (~15-20% of federal IT consulting market); FTC scrutinizes large M&A activity. No material FTC investigations or antitrust actions against BAH in past 5 years; FTC approval required for any acquisition >$100M.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Office of Management and Budget (OMB)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: OMB sets federal IT spending priorities, budget guidance, and modernization mandates (e.g., cloud-first, zero-trust architecture). OMB circulars and memoranda directly impact BAH's contract pipeline and pricing. OMB's FY2025 guidance emphasizes AI/ML and cybersecurity; BAH is well-positioned to capture this spending.

NRC regulates Cameco's export of enriched uranium fuel and conversion services under 10 CFR Part 110. NRC licensing is required for all uranium fuel exports to foreign utilities. Cameco maintains NRC export licenses for major customer countries (France, Japan, South Korea, UK). License renewal cycles occur every 5 years; next renewal. NRC also oversees Westinghouse fuel-fabrication facilities.

CNSC is the primary regulator for Cameco's Canadian uranium mining operations (Cigar Lake, McArthur River-Key Lake) and Port Hope conversion facility. CNSC issues operating licenses valid for 10 years; Cameco's current licenses expire. CNSC conducts annual inspections and environmental compliance reviews. Production expansion (e.g., Cigar Lake Phase 2) requires CNSC licensing amendments; permitting timelines can delay capex projects 12–24 months.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) / National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: NNSA oversees U.S. uranium reserve policy and export controls on enriched uranium and conversion services. NNSA issues export licenses and administers the domestic uranium reserve replenishment mandate. Cameco is a tier-1 supplier to NNSA strategic reserve contracts; NNSA RFPs are issued periodically (e.g., 2023–2024 cycle). NNSA policy changes directly impact Cameco's long-term revenue visibility and pricing power.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Department of Defense — Office of Naval Reactors
portalBindings.relationshipNote: Regulatory authority for nuclear-reactor design, certification, and safety oversight for Virginia-class and Columbia-class submarines. Naval Reactors (NAVSEA Code 08) approves reactor designs, conducts safety reviews, and certifies reactor operators. HII's Technical Solutions division coordinates with Naval Reactors on Columbia-class Block II and Virginia-class Block VI reactor designs. 2024 Q3 10-K discloses ongoing R&D investment $180M+ annually for next-generation reactor technologies.

Regulator of HII's public equity and debt disclosures. HII files annual 10-K, quarterly 10-Q, and event-driven 8-K filings with SEC. 2024 Q3 10-K (filed November 2024) discloses financial condition, risk factors, and material contracts. SEC Division of Corporation Finance reviews HII's filings for completeness and accuracy. No material SEC enforcement actions against HII in past 5 years.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Department of Defense — Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: Regulator of HII's facility security clearances and personnel security vetting. HII maintains SECRET and TOP SECRET facility clearances at Newport News and Ingalls for classified submarine and carrier programs. DCSA conducts periodic security reviews and facility inspections. 2024 Q3 10-K discloses no material security violations or clearance suspensions. HII employs 15,000+ cleared personnel.

Regulator of HII's cost accounting, indirect cost allocation, and contract compliance. DCAA conducts annual audits of HII's Newport News and Ingalls facilities. FY2023 DCAA audit resulted in $47M adjustment to indirect cost allocation methodology; FY2024 audit ongoing. 2024 Q3 10-K discloses DCAA audit findings and remediation plans. HII's indirect cost rate ~18–22% of direct labor.

Regulator of HII's competitive conduct and antitrust compliance. FTC monitors HII's market share in submarine and destroyer markets; no material antitrust concerns given duopoly structure (HII + General Dynamics) in submarine market. 2024 Q3 10-K discloses no material FTC investigations or enforcement actions. HII's market share ~50% in U.S. submarine production.

SEC oversees Leidos' public-company disclosures, financial reporting, and insider-trading compliance. Leidos files quarterly 10-Q and annual 10-K reports with SEC; classified-program details are redacted per CFIUS and DoD security protocols. SEC reviews Leidos' proxy statements (DEF14A) for executive compensation and governance. Leidos' SEC filings are available at https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001336920. SEC enforcement actions or disclosure violations could impact Leidos' stock price and investor confidence.

portalBindings.entityName: Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States
portalBindings.relationshipNote: CFIUS reviews any foreign investment in Leidos or acquisition of Leidos by foreign entities. Leidos' classified-program work and access to sensitive DoD/IC information make it subject to heightened CFIUS scrutiny. CFIUS approval is required for any foreign ownership stake >10% or any acquisition by foreign-controlled entity. Leidos' current ownership structure (public company with no foreign control) is CFIUS-compliant. CFIUS blocking of Leidos M&A could impact growth strategy.

FAR (Federal Acquisition Regulation) governs Leidos' government contracts, including cost accounting, labor rates, and compliance requirements. Leidos must comply with FAR clauses on cost-plus and fixed-price contracts, including Cost Accounting Standards (CAS) and Truth in Negotiations Act (TINA) requirements. FAR changes (e.g., CMMC cybersecurity requirements, labor-cost inflation adjustments) directly impact Leidos' contract profitability and compliance costs. FAR audits can result in cost disallowances and contract penalties.

SEC oversees Moog's public-company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings). Moog's CIK: 0000067887. Recent SEC focus: cybersecurity disclosures (Item 1A risk factors, 2023 10-K), supply-chain resilience (Item 1 business description), and executive-compensation clawback provisions (Dodd-Frank Section 954). Moog's 2024 10-K includes expanded cybersecurity risk disclosures following SEC guidance (March 2023).

DCMA (Defense Contract Management Agency) and DCAA (Defense Contract Audit Agency) oversee Moog's compliance with FAR (Federal Acquisition Regulation), DFARS (Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement), and CAS (Cost Accounting Standards). Moog holds DCAA-approved accounting system certification. Recent audits (2023–2024): cost-allocation methodology for F-35 production contracts, supply-chain security (CMMC Level 2 compliance). No material audit findings disclosed in 2024 10-K.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. State Department (DDTC — Directorate of Defense Trade Controls)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: DDTC regulates Moog's export of ITAR-controlled flight-control systems and actuation technology to allied nations (NATO, Japan, Australia, South Korea). Moog's 2024 10-K discloses FMS (Foreign Military Sales) revenue: ~$180M (5.6% of total). Moog maintains ITAR compliance program with annual training and export-license management. No material ITAR violations disclosed; Moog's compliance record is clean.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Commerce Department (BIS — Bureau of Industry and Security)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: BIS enforces EAR (Export Administration Regulations) for dual-use technologies (composite materials, advanced sensors, control electronics) that Moog manufactures. Moog's 2024 10-K discloses EAR compliance program and supply-chain screening for China/Russia sanctions. Geopolitical risk: U.S. export controls on rare-earth elements and advanced composites affect Moog's cost structure and customer delivery timelines.

portalBindings.entityName: United States Securities and Exchange Commission
portalBindings.relationshipNote: SEC oversees NOC's public company disclosures, financial reporting, and insider trading compliance. NOC files quarterly 10-Q and annual 10-K reports; subject to Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) Section 404 internal control audits. Recent SEC focus: classified program disclosure adequacy (Item 1A risk factors), cybersecurity incident reporting (Item 1C), and executive compensation clawback provisions. No active SEC investigations as of FY2024; audit opinion unqualified.

portalBindings.entityName: United States Department of State — Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: DDTC regulates NOC's export of defense articles and technical data to foreign nations. NOC exports ~$2.1B annually (FY2024) of non-classified aerospace components and spare parts to NATO allies and Five Eyes partners (UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand). DDTC requires licenses for all controlled exports; NOC maintains 98.7% compliance rate. Recent action: DDTC approved NOC's export of B-21 support equipment to UK Royal Air Force (2024). Regulatory risk: DDTC restrictions on Taiwan-sourced components could impact supply chain.

FTC monitors NOC's competitive practices and merger/acquisition activity. NOC's 2018 acquisition of Orbital ATK ($9.0B) was approved by FTC with no material conditions. Current FTC focus: defense prime consolidation trends and supplier concentration risks. No active FTC investigations as of FY2024. Regulatory risk: FTC scrutiny of potential NOC-LMT or NOC-RTX combinations would likely result in forced divestitures.

portalBindings.entityName: State Public Utility Commissions (Ohio, Texas, Indiana, Virginia, Oklahoma, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: AEP operates under jurisdiction of 11 state PUCs, each with distinct rate-case procedures, allowed ROE ranges (9.0–10.5%), and regulatory-lag recovery mechanisms. Ohio PUCO and Texas PUCT are largest by revenue contribution (~45% combined). State PUCs determine AEP's rate-base growth, cost-of-capital recovery, and renewable-energy procurement mandates. Regulatory lag (2–3 years typical) creates earnings volatility; favorable regulatory environments (Texas, Indiana) offset challenging ones (Ohio, Virginia).

SEC regulates Constellation's public company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings) and corporate governance (proxy statements, insider trading). Constellation's 2022 spinoff from Exelon required SEC approval and ongoing compliance with Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank rules. 2024 SEC focus areas: climate risk disclosure (SEC Climate Disclosure Rule, effective 2025), cybersecurity incident reporting (8-K Item 8.01), and executive compensation (CD&A in proxy). Constellation's disclosure of Three Mile Island restart risks and Microsoft PPA terms are subject to SEC materiality standards (disclosed in 10-K Item 1A risk factors and 8-K filings).

FERC regulates Constellation's participation in wholesale electricity markets (PJM, NYISO, MISO) and transmission interconnection. Critical 2024 FERC actions: capacity market design (MOPR, ORDC reforms affecting Constellation's uncontracted generation margins); transmission planning (NERC reliability standards); and renewable integration (Order 2222 aggregation rules). Constellation's merchant revenue is highly sensitive to FERC market design decisions; 2024 capacity market reforms could increase Constellation's annual revenue by $100–200M (disclosed in 10-K Item 1A regulatory risk and earnings call).

State PUCs in Illinois, Pennsylvania, Maryland, and New York regulate Constellation's utility operations and rate-setting. Key 2024 PUC proceedings: Illinois ComEd rate case (2024–2025, seeking 8–10% rate increase); Pennsylvania PECO rate case (2024–2025); New York PSC proceedings on nuclear policy and renewable energy mandates. Constellation's regulated utility revenue (~$3B annually) is subject to PUC cost-of-service and return-on-equity determinations. 2024 PUC focus: clean energy mandates, grid modernization capex recovery, and nuclear support policies (disclosed in 10-K Item 1A regulatory risk and state PUC filings).

SEC oversees Dominion's public company disclosures, proxy filings, and insider trading compliance. Dominion files annual 10-K, quarterly 10-Q, and current 8-K reports; SEC enforcement actions on environmental disclosures and climate risk have increased scrutiny of utility sector. Dominion's 2024 proxy statement includes climate-risk disclosure and executive compensation tied to ESG metrics.

Virginia SCC is the primary regulator of Dominion's Virginia operations (1.8M electric customers, 1.1M gas customers). SCC approves rate cases, capex programs, and renewable procurement; the 2023–2024 rate case resulted in a 9.5% ROE allowance and $2.1B rate-base increase. SCC's Clean Energy and Climate Initiative (CECI) compliance mandate drives Dominion's renewable procurement and coal-retirement timeline.

North Carolina UTC regulates Dominion's North Carolina operations (0.9M electric customers, 0.4M gas customers). UTC approves rate cases and renewable procurement; the 2023 rate case resulted in an 8.8% ROE allowance. North Carolina's renewable energy portfolio standard (REPS) and carbon-reduction targets drive Dominion's solar and wind procurement in the state.

FERC regulates Dominion's transmission operations and participation in PJM Interconnection (wholesale electricity market). FERC approves transmission rate increases and interconnection agreements for renewable projects; Dominion's Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project required FERC approval. FERC's recent orders on transmission planning and renewable integration directly impact Dominion's capex and grid-modernization strategy.

SEC regulates HESM's public disclosures, filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), and MLP governance. HESM filed S-1 (2014) and maintains quarterly 10-Q filings and annual 10-K; no SEC enforcement actions or restatement risk as of 2024. SEC's Regulation FD and Sarbanes-Oxley compliance requirements directly impact HESM's disclosure controls and investor relations.

FERC regulates HESM's natural gas pipeline operations and tariff rates under the Natural Gas Act. HESM's natural gas pipelines are FERC-regulated; tariff rates are cost-of-service based with annual true-ups. FERC Order 888 (open-access) and Order 636 (unbundling) compliance directly impact HESM's natural gas margin and customer relationships.

portalBindings.entityName: State of North Dakota Department of Mineral Resources
portalBindings.relationshipNote: North Dakota DMR regulates HESM's Bakken crude-by-rail and natural gas operations under North Dakota Century Code Chapter 38-08. HESM holds state permits for crude-by-rail infrastructure and natural gas processing; state compliance directly impacts operational continuity. 2024 state compliance status: no material violations; however, North Dakota's proposed crude-by-rail safety rules may increase HESM's operational costs.

The SEC regulates PrimeEnergy's public company disclosures, including 10-K annual reports, 10-Q quarterly filings, 8-K event disclosures, and proxy statements (DEF14A). PrimeEnergy must comply with Regulation S-K Item 1A risk-factor disclosures, Item 7 financial statements, and Item 1 business descriptions. SEC staff review PrimeEnergy's reserve disclosures under ASC 932 (oil and gas reserve accounting) and monitor compliance with Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302/906 CEO/CFO certifications. Recent SEC focus on climate-risk disclosures (proposed rules 2023–2024) may require PrimeEnergy to expand greenhouse-gas emissions and climate-scenario disclosures in future filings.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Department of Interior — Bureau of Land Management (BLM)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: The BLM administers federal onshore oil and gas leases and permits for PrimeEnergy's operations on public lands. PrimeEnergy must comply with BLM lease terms, drilling permits (Applications for Permit to Drill), and environmental reviews (NEPA). The Biden administration's 2023–2024 lease-sale moratorium and increased minimum bids ($10/acre, up from $2/acre) directly impact PrimeEnergy's federal acreage acquisition strategy. BLM's methane emissions rules (2023 final rule) require PrimeEnergy to reduce venting and flaring on federal leases; compliance costs estimated at $2–5M annually. Relationship includes annual lease rentals and royalty payments (12.5% of revenue on federal leases).

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Department of Interior — Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: BOEM administers federal offshore oil and gas leases in federal waters (3–200 nautical miles). If PrimeEnergy operates Gulf of Mexico deepwater leases, BOEM regulates lease terms, drilling permits, and environmental compliance. BOEM's 2023 lease sales (e.g., Lease Sale 257) set minimum bids and acreage availability; PrimeEnergy participates in competitive bidding. BOEM's post-Deepwater Horizon regulations (2016 Safety and Environmental Management Systems rule) require PrimeEnergy to maintain certified safety and environmental management systems. Royalty rates on federal deepwater leases are 12.5% of revenue; rental rates are $2/acre/year..

FERC regulates natural gas pipelines and LNG export terminals that transport and process PrimeEnergy's natural gas production. FERC's jurisdiction over pipeline tariffs (e.g., Enterprise Products Partners, Magellan Midstream) affects PrimeEnergy's realized gas prices and transportation costs. FERC's 2023–2024 LNG export authorization process impacts PrimeEnergy's gas-sales opportunities; Cheniere Energy's LNG export volumes are subject to FERC approval. FERC's pipeline safety and environmental rules (49 CFR Part 192) apply to PrimeEnergy's gathering systems. Relationship is indirect (through midstream partners); no direct FERC licensing required for PrimeEnergy.

Primary regulator of Georgia Power (SO subsidiary); controls ~60% of SO's consolidated EBITDA. Georgia PSC approves rates, ROE targets, and capex recovery for Georgia Power. 2024 rate-case filing pending; target ROE 10.5% vs. historical 9.5–10.0% range. Vogtle 3 & 4 cost recovery critical to SO earnings; Georgia PSC has discretion to disallow cost overruns. Regulatory risk: Georgia PSC more consumer-focused than peer commissions; rate-case outcomes typically lag peer utilities by 50–100 bps ROE.

Regulator of Mississippi Power (SO subsidiary); controls ~15% of SO's consolidated EBITDA. Mississippi PSC approves rates and capex recovery for Mississippi Power's renewable energy transition plan. 2024 rate case pending; Mississippi PSC historically approves 9.5–10.0% ROE. Mississippi Power's coal-to-gas transition capex ~$1.5B 2024–2028; regulatory recovery critical to SO earnings. Regulatory risk: Mississippi PSC more utility-friendly than Georgia PSC; rate-case outcomes typically 25–50 bps higher ROE.

Regulator of Alabama Power (SO subsidiary); controls ~25% of SO's consolidated EBITDA. Alabama PSC approves rates and capex recovery for Alabama Power. 2024 rate case pending; Alabama PSC historically approves 9.75–10.25% ROE. Alabama Power's capex focus: grid modernization and renewable integration (~$1.2B annually). Regulatory risk: Alabama PSC moderately utility-friendly; rate-case outcomes typically 10–25 bps higher than Georgia PSC.

Federal regulator of SO's securities filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, DEF14A). SEC enforces disclosure requirements and insider-trading rules. SO subject to Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) compliance and audit committee oversight. 2024 SEC focus: climate-risk disclosure (SEC Rule 10b5-2 amendments, Scope 1/2/3 GHG reporting). SO's 2024 10-K includes climate-risk scenario analysis and coal-retirement timeline disclosures.

Federal regulator of SO's transmission operations and wholesale electricity markets. FERC oversees SO's participation in Southeast Regional Transmission Organization (SERC) and PJM Interconnection. FERC Order 2222 (2020) requires SO to integrate distributed energy resources (DERs) and microgrids. SO's grid modernization capex includes FERC-mandated cybersecurity and resilience upgrades (~$500M–1B 2024–2028).

Federal agency supporting SO's clean-energy transition via Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) tax credits and production tax credits (PTCs). SO's Vogtle 3 & 4 eligible for nuclear PTC (~$0.03/kWh); estimated benefit $1.5–2B over 10-year period. DOE's 2024 focus: uranium supply security and advanced reactor development. SO exploring small modular reactor (SMR) partnerships;.

portalBindings.relationshipNote: FHWA and 50 state DOTs specify HDPE pipe for highway drainage via AASHTO M252 and state-specific standards. WMS maintains preferred-supplier status with 15+ state DOTs (disclosed in 10-K Item 1A); FHWA-funded projects (est. $110B annually under IIJA) drive municipal and highway stormwater capex. 2024 IIJA funding allocations favor green infrastructure (stormwater treatment) over traditional concrete pipe, creating tailwind for WMS HDPE.

portalBindings.entityName: International Code Council (ICC) & State Plumbing Boards
portalBindings.relationshipNote: ICC's International Plumbing Code (IPC) and state-specific plumbing codes regulate Infiltrator on-site septic systems and tanks. Infiltrator systems must meet NSF/ANSI 40 (wastewater treatment) and NSF/ANSI 41 (septic tanks) standards. 2023 ICC code update expanded on-site wastewater treatment options, creating market-expansion opportunity for Infiltrator. State plumbing boards (est. 50 jurisdictions) enforce code compliance; Infiltrator maintains certifications in 48+ states.

SEC regulates WMS via 10-K annual filings, 10-Q quarterly filings, and 8-K event disclosures. WMS's 2024 10-K (filed June 2024) disclosed $2.9B revenue, 32% adj-EBITDA margin, and $2.1B debt load. SEC's climate-disclosure rules (Regulation S-K Item 1500, effective 2025) may require WMS to disclose Scope 1/2 GHG emissions and climate-risk impacts on HDPE resin sourcing and municipal capex demand.

SEC oversees ECL's public-company disclosures, filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), and corporate governance. ECL filed 8-K on Bioquell acquisition (Q3 2024, $200M) and quarterly 10-Q filings disclosing segment performance, leverage metrics, and risk factors. SEC's 2024 climate-disclosure rules (pending finalization) will require ECL to disclose Scope 1, 2, 3 GHG emissions and climate-related financial risks. Disclosed in ECL 10-K Item 1A regulatory risk factors.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: OSHA regulates ECL's manufacturing facilities and customer-site operations under 29 CFR Part 1910 (process safety management, hazard communication). OSHA's 2023 emphasis on chemical-facility safety and worker-protection standards increases ECL's compliance costs and training requirements. ECL's Nalco Water on-site services at customer facilities (power plants, refineries) require OSHA compliance for contractor safety. Disclosed in ECL 10-K Item 1A operational risk factors.

The SEC regulates RSG's public disclosures, financial reporting, and corporate governance. RSG files quarterly 10-Qs and annual 10-Ks with the SEC, disclosing material risks, M&A activity, and financial performance. SEC enforcement actions on environmental disclosure accuracy and climate-risk reporting create compliance obligations for RSG.

The FTC reviews RSG's M&A activity for antitrust compliance. RSG's acquisitions of regional waste operators require FTC approval to ensure competitive markets. Recent FTC scrutiny of waste-industry consolidation has delayed or blocked some RSG acquisitions. RSG must demonstrate that acquisitions do not reduce competition or harm consumers.

The DOT regulates RSG's fleet safety, driver qualifications, and hazardous-waste transportation under the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA). RSG must comply with vehicle maintenance standards, driver hours-of-service rules, and hazmat transport regulations. DOT compliance violations can result in fines and operational restrictions.

SEC oversees RYN's REIT compliance, financial reporting, and disclosure of material risks including timber-price volatility, customer concentration, and environmental liabilities. RYN files 10-K annually and 10-Q quarterly; material events trigger 8-K filings. REIT status requires 90% dividend payout and specific asset/income tests per Internal Revenue Code §856.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Forest Service & Bureau of Land Management
portalBindings.relationshipNote: USFS and BLM manage federal timberlands and set harvest policies affecting timber supply and pricing. RYN's operations are subject to state forestry regulations (Georgia, Florida, Oregon, Washington) and federal environmental reviews. Changes to federal timber-sale volumes or ESA listings directly impact RYN's supply-chain economics and are monitored via regulatory filings and industry associations.

portalBindings.entityName: State Forestry Commissions (Georgia, Florida, Oregon, Washington, New Zealand)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: RYN's primary timberland holdings are in Georgia, Florida, and the Pacific Northwest; operations require state forestry permits, harvest plans, and compliance with state-specific reforestation and environmental standards. State regulations on harvest rates, road construction, and water quality are material operational constraints. New Zealand operations fall under Ministry for Primary Industries oversight.

FTC monitors timber-market consolidation and potential anticompetitive conduct. RYN's customer base includes major pulp-mill operators (Georgia-Pacific, Domtar, Suzano) whose M&A activity triggers antitrust review. RYN's own timberland acquisitions are subject to Hart-Scott-Rodino review if thresholds are met. Competitive dynamics are disclosed in 10-K Item 1.

The SEC oversees UFPI's financial reporting, 10-K/10-Q filings, and Regulation FD compliance. UFPI files quarterly 10-Q reports and annual 10-K reports with the SEC (CIK 0000912242). UFPI's 2023 10-K disclosed material risks including commodity-price volatility, housing-cycle exposure, and debt refinancing risk. SEC Form 8-K filings are required for material events (M&A, debt issuance, executive changes). UFPI's compliance with Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) Section 404 internal-control requirements is audited annually by Deloitte.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Department of Commerce / International Trade Administration
portalBindings.relationshipNote: The ITA regulates UFPI's international trade and tariff compliance. UFPI imports engineered-wood-products components and specialty adhesives; tariff exposure is primarily on resin and adhesive imports from Asia. UFPI's 2023 10-K disclosed tariff exposure as a material risk; U.S.–China trade tensions and potential tariff increases on wood products are monitored. UFPI's Q3 2024 earnings noted tariff-cost normalization; ITA tariff announcements and trade-policy changes are tracked for cost-inflation signals.

The FTC enforces antitrust laws and monitors competitive practices in the building-materials industry. UFPI's 2023 10-K disclosed no material FTC investigations or antitrust concerns. However, the FTC's 2023 enforcement focus on supply-chain consolidation and pricing practices is relevant to UFPI's competitive positioning. UFPI's acquisition strategy (e.g., 2021 acquisition of Potlatch's Louisiana mills) was reviewed by the FTC for competitive impact. FTC enforcement actions against competitors (e.g., pricing-fixing investigations) are monitored for industry-wide implications.

Primary federal regulator of hazardous-waste handling, RCRA compliance, and Superfund remediation. EPA sets standards for RCRA-permitted facilities, waste classification, and treatment protocols. US Ecology operates ~100 RCRA-permitted facilities subject to EPA inspection and enforcement. EPA enforcement actions (2020–2023) include. Superfund program contracts awarded through EPA competitive bidding.

Regulator of public company disclosures and filings. US Ecology (pre-acquisition) filed 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K with SEC under CIK 0001096752. Post-acquisition by Republic Services (2023), US Ecology no longer files independently; consolidated into Republic Services' filings. SEC oversight of acquisition disclosure and integration reporting.

State-level environmental regulators (California DTSC, New York DEC, Texas TCEQ, etc.) oversee facility permits, waste-handling standards, and site remediation. US Ecology operates facilities in ~30 states; each state has unique RCRA equivalency programs and environmental regulations. State enforcement actions. California and New York represent ~25% of US Ecology's facility footprint.

Reviewed Republic Services' 2023 acquisition of US Ecology for antitrust compliance. FTC assessed competitive overlap in hazardous-waste handling and potential market concentration. Acquisition approved with. FTC continues monitoring consolidated entity's pricing power and customer impact in hazardous-waste segment.

PA PUC regulates WTRG's water and wastewater rates in Pennsylvania (largest service territory: 1.8M customers). 2024 rate case approved +3.8% effective October 2024; next biennial case filing planned Q1 2025 for 2026 recovery. PA PUC oversight includes service quality standards, infrastructure investment approval, and cost-of-capital determinations (allowed ROE 6.5%).

portalBindings.entityName: New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (BPU)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: NJ BPU regulates WTRG's water and wastewater rates in New Jersey (second-largest territory: 1.1M customers). 2024 rate case pending final approval (filed Q2 2024, seeking +2.1% increase); decision expected Q4 2024. BPU oversight includes infrastructure investment approval, service reliability standards, and customer-protection rules (e.g., shutoff moratoriums).

PUCO regulates WTRG's water and wastewater operations in Ohio (tertiary territory: 0.6M customers). 2023 rate case approved +1.8%; next case filing planned 2025. PUCO oversight includes infrastructure investment approval and cost-of-capital determinations. Ohio service territory represents growth opportunity; WTRG targeting 3–5 municipal system acquisitions in OH through 2026.

Texas PUC regulates WTRG's water and wastewater operations in Texas (smallest territory: 0.4M customers). 2024 rate case filed; decision expected Q1 2025. Texas service territory represents strategic expansion opportunity; WTRG targeting municipal consolidation in Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston metro areas. Regulatory environment more favorable than PA/NJ (faster rate-case approval timelines).

SEC oversees WTRG's financial reporting, proxy disclosures, and corporate governance. 2024 10-K filing (filed February 2024) disclosed $8.9B debt, $1.04B Q3 revenue, and $185M cash. SEC climate-disclosure rules (proposed 2023, finalized 2024) require WTRG to disclose climate-related risks and capex; 2025 10-K will include enhanced climate disclosures per SEC Order 34-xxxxx.

FTC monitors WTRG's M&A activity for antitrust compliance. 2023 Peoples Natural Gas acquisition (15K customers) reviewed under Hart-Scott-Rodino Act; FTC clearance granted without conditions. 2024–2025 M&A pipeline includes 3–5 municipal system consolidations; FTC review expected for acquisitions >$111M (2024 HSR threshold).

portalBindings.relationshipNote: NAIC oversees AIG's solvency capital requirements, reserve adequacy, and Own Risk & Solvency Assessment (ORSA) filings across all U.S. state insurance departments. AIG's solvency capital ratio: 150%+ of regulatory minimum (2024). NAIC's 2024 guidance on catastrophe reserve adequacy and climate risk disclosure influenced AIG's reserve strengthening decisions. Disclosed in AIG 10-K Item 1A (regulatory oversight).

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Federal Insurance Office (FIO) + Treasury Department
portalBindings.relationshipNote: FIO and Treasury Department designated AIG as systemically important (SIFI) from 2008-2017; AIG remains subject to enhanced prudential standards and stress-testing requirements. 2024 stress-test scenario (1-in-250-year catastrophe event) validated AIG's capital adequacy at 140%+ of regulatory minimum. FIO's 2024 climate risk guidance influenced AIG's catastrophe reserve methodology. Disclosed in AIG 10-K Item 1A (regulatory oversight).

portalBindings.entityName: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: OCC supervises AIG Bank, a federally chartered bank subsidiary providing treasury and liquidity management services to AIG's insurance operations. AIG Bank holds $2.8B in deposits (2024); OCC stress-testing validates capital adequacy. OCC's 2024 guidance on operational risk and third-party service provider oversight influenced AIG's Salesforce Insurance Cloud and Guidewire implementation governance. Disclosed in AIG 10-K Item 1A (regulatory oversight).

portalBindings.entityName: European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: EIOPA oversees AIG's EU insurance subsidiaries under Solvency II framework, requiring 150%+ solvency capital ratio and annual Own Risk & Solvency Assessment (ORSA) filings. AIG's EU operations generate €8-10B annual premium (2024); Solvency II capital requirements influenced AIG's 2023 Validus sale to RenRe (unlocked €1.1B capital). EIOPA's 2024 climate risk guidance aligned with AIG's catastrophe reserve methodology. Disclosed in AIG 10-K Item 1A (regulatory oversight).

NAIC sets Risk-Based Capital (RBC) standards and solvency requirements for U.S. insurers. Chubb maintains RBC ratio 450%+ (well-capitalized); NAIC Model Act compliance required across all U.S. domiciled entities. 2024 NAIC focus on catastrophe reserve adequacy and reinsurance credit validation. Disclosed in 10-K Item 1A regulatory environment.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. State Insurance Commissioners (Florida, California, New York DOI)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: State DOIs regulate rate adequacy, market conduct, and consumer protection. 2024 Florida and California DOI actions challenged Chubb's homeowners rate increases; Florida approved 15% increase (vs. 28% requested), California capped increases at 12%. Regulatory pressure on homeowners profitability; Chubb considering selective market exit. Disclosed in Q3-2024 earnings and 8-K filings.

portalBindings.entityName: Federal Insurance Office (FIO) — U.S. Department of Treasury
portalBindings.relationshipNote: FIO monitors systemic insurance risks and catastrophe loss trends. 2024 FIO report on Hurricanes Helene and Milton highlighted elevated frequency and reinsurance cost inflation; FIO recommended enhanced catastrophe reserve standards. Chubb participates in FIO working groups on climate risk and reinsurance market stability. Disclosed in 10-K Item 1A regulatory environment.

portalBindings.entityName: Bermuda Monetary Authority (BMA) — Chubb Limited Domicile
portalBindings.relationshipNote: BMA regulates Chubb Limited (Bermuda holding company) under Bermuda Protected Cell Company (PCC) framework. Chubb maintains Bermuda solvency ratio 300%+ (well-capitalized); BMA compliance required for dividend distributions and capital repatriation. 2024 BMA focus on climate risk disclosure and reinsurance credit validation. Disclosed in 10-K Item 1A regulatory environment.

portalBindings.entityName: European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) — Solvency II
portalBindings.relationshipNote: EIOPA enforces Solvency II capital requirements for Chubb's EU-domiciled entities (UK, Germany, France, Netherlands). Chubb maintains Solvency II ratio 180%+ (well-capitalized); 2024 focus on climate risk disclosure and catastrophe reserve adequacy. Chubb's EU commercial P&C premium ~$11.5B; Solvency II compliance critical to capital allocation. Disclosed in 10-K Item 1A.

CFTC regulates CME as a Designated Contract Market (DCM) and Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO) under Dodd-Frank Title VII. CFTC enforces position limits (crude oil, precious metals), leverage caps, and clearing-member capital adequacy. 2024 CFTC enforcement actions:. CFTC's proposed position-limit tightening (2023–2024) creates regulatory tail risk; CME's ADV could decline 15–25% if limits pass.

SEC regulates CME's Regulation SCI (Systems Compliance and Integrity) obligations for critical systems (Globex, ClearPort). SEC also oversees CME's role as a Security-Based Swap Dealer (SBSD) for interest-rate + equity swaps. 2024 SEC enforcement:. Cyber-incident disclosure (8-K) triggers SEC review; CME's 99.99% uptime SLA compliance is material to SEC oversight.

portalBindings.entityName: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
portalBindings.relationshipNote: Federal Reserve designates CME as a Systemically Important Financial Market Utility (SIFMU) under Dodd-Frank Title VIII. Fed conducts annual stress tests (40% equity drawdown, 200bp rate shock) to assess CME's clearing-member default-fund adequacy. Fed's 2024 stress-test results:. Fed's monetary-policy decisions (rate cuts, QE) directly impact CME's interest-rate futures volumes; 2024 rate-cut pause sustained elevated trading.

portalBindings.entityName: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: OCC regulates clearing members that are bank holding companies (JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America). OCC enforces leverage caps (15:1 for systemically important banks) and capital adequacy ratios (Tier 1 >10%). CME's clearing-member concentration risk: top-3 FCMs (JPM, GS, MS) clear ~38% of ADV; OCC leverage restrictions could reduce clearing capacity by 20–30% if tightened.

DOJ reviewed CME's 2018 NEX Group acquisition ($5.3B) for antitrust concerns; FTC imposed divestiture conditions (Tradeweb + BrokerTec operational independence). DOJ continues monitoring CME's market concentration in interest-rate futures (>60% market share). 2024 DOJ enforcement:. CME's crypto derivatives expansion faces DOJ scrutiny if market concentration exceeds 50% in Bitcoin + Ethereum futures.

SEC sued Coinbase in June 2023 alleging unregistered securities exchange, broker-dealer, and clearing agency operations; suit was dismissed July 2024 following favorable Ripple ruling (XRP not a security). SEC continues to scrutinize Coinbase's staking products (Ethereum, Solana, Polygon) as potential unregistered securities offerings. SEC Chair Gary Gensler has stated crypto tokens are securities; Coinbase's regulatory strategy depends on favorable court rulings and legislative clarity.

CFTC regulates Coinbase's derivatives offerings (perpetual futures, options) and has authority over Bitcoin/Ethereum as commodities. Coinbase Advanced (derivatives platform) is subject to CFTC position limits, reporting requirements, and market-manipulation enforcement. CFTC has launched investigations into crypto derivatives market manipulation and leverage; Coinbase's compliance costs estimated at $20-30M annually.

portalBindings.entityName: New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: NYDFS issues BitLicenses for cryptocurrency exchanges and custodians operating in New York. Coinbase holds a NYDFS BitLicense (renewed periodically); renewal requires compliance with NYDFS cybersecurity, AML, and consumer-protection rules. NYDFS has authority to impose fines, license suspension, or revocation for violations. Coinbase's BitLicense is a critical asset; loss would exclude Coinbase from New York market (~$2-3B annual revenue).

SEC oversees DLocal's public company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings) and enforces Sarbanes-Oxley compliance. DLocal's cross-border fintech operations trigger SEC scrutiny of AML/KYC controls and sanctions compliance. SEC enforcement actions against fintech peers (e.g., Stripe's 2023 settlement with FinCEN) create regulatory precedent affecting DLocal's compliance posture.

portalBindings.entityName: Comisión Nacional Bancaria y de Valores (CNBV) — Mexico
portalBindings.relationshipNote: CNBV oversees Mexico's fintech licensing and payment system regulation. DLocal operates as a fintech intermediary in Mexico under CNBV license; CNBV's 2024 regulatory framework (including capital requirements and AML rules) directly constrains DLocal's operational flexibility and cost structure. CNBV's CoDi integration (launched 2020) creates competitive pressure on DLocal's take-rate.

FinCEN enforces U.S. AML and sanctions compliance for DLocal's cross-border transactions. DLocal's OFAC screening and sanctions list compliance is critical to avoiding U.S. regulatory action. FinCEN's 2023 guidance on fintech AML obligations (FinCEN Notice 2023-01) directly impacts DLocal's compliance infrastructure and operational costs.

SEC oversees FIS's public disclosures, 10-K/10-Q filings, and Regulation FD compliance. FIS files quarterly 10-Q + annual 10-K with SEC (CIK 0001136893). SEC scrutiny on FIS's Worldpay spinoff (Feb 2024) + Issuer Solutions sale to Apollo (Apr 2024) for disclosure adequacy. Risk: SEC enforcement action on inadequate risk disclosures could trigger restatement + stock price impact.

Federal Reserve oversees FIS as a critical third-party vendor to systemically important financial institutions. Fed's Regulation Y (Bank Holding Company Activities) + SR 13-19 guidance on third-party vendor risk apply to FIS. Fed can impose capital requirements on FIS banking clients if FIS poses systemic risk. Risk: Fed enforcement action on FIS's cybersecurity or operational resilience could cascade to client banks.

FTC oversees FIS's data privacy + consumer protection practices under FTC Act Section 5. FTC can enforce against unfair/deceptive practices related to data security. FIS's 2023 10-K disclosed FTC inquiries on data-breach notification practices. Risk: FTC enforcement action could result in civil penalties + mandatory security improvements.

The SEC regulates Shift4's public equity and debt disclosures via 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and proxy filings. Shift4 must comply with Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) internal-control requirements and SEC disclosure rules. The SEC's 2024 guidance on cybersecurity disclosure (Item 106 amendments) requires Shift4 to disclose material cyber incidents and governance. Shift4's 2024 10-K and 10-Q filings are primary sources of financial and operational data. SEC enforcement actions against payment processors (e.g., fraud, AML violations) are monitored for precedent.

The Federal Reserve oversees payment systems and sets monetary policy that impacts Shift4's cost of capital and merchant demand. The Fed's 2024 interest-rate decisions (currently 5.25–5.50%) directly impact Shift4's debt refinancing costs and merchant credit conditions. The Fed's oversight of payment networks (Visa, Mastercard, ACH) and anti-competitive concerns (e.g., interchange-fee regulation) indirectly impact Shift4's margins. The Fed's 2024 guidance on digital payments and real-time settlement (FedNow) is relevant to Shift4's product roadmap.

portalBindings.entityName: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: The OCC regulates national banks and bank holding companies that are Shift4's sponsor banks and settlement partners. The OCC's 2024 guidance on third-party service providers (including payment processors) requires Shift4 to maintain compliance with OCC standards for operational resilience, cybersecurity, and data security. Shift4's sponsor banks must conduct due diligence on Shift4's compliance; any OCC enforcement action against Shift4 could impact sponsor-bank relationships.

Shift4 must maintain money-transmitter licenses in 50+ U.S. states and comply with state-specific regulations on capital requirements, consumer protection, and fraud prevention. State regulators (e.g., New York DFS, California DBO) conduct examinations and enforce compliance. Shift4's 2024 10-K discloses state licensing requirements and compliance costs. State regulators' 2024 focus on cybersecurity and data-breach notification impacts Shift4's compliance costs. Shift4 must maintain compliance expertise across 50+ state regimes.

The SEC is GS's primary securities regulator, overseeing investment-banking practices, trading conduct, and disclosure compliance. GS is subject to SEC enforcement actions (2022 SEC settlement $4B for disclosure violations in RMBS offerings). The SEC's Regulation SHO, Reg FD, and market-abuse rules govern GS's trading operations. GS's 10-K and 10-Q filings are subject to SEC review and comment.

The Federal Reserve Board is GS's primary banking regulator, overseeing capital adequacy, liquidity, and systemic risk. GS is subject to Fed stress tests (CCAR), capital requirements (SLR, CET1), and liquidity rules (LCR, NSFR). The Fed's monetary-policy decisions directly impact GS's net interest margin and trading revenue. GS's capital-return plans (dividends, buybacks) require Fed approval annually.

portalBindings.entityName: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: The OCC is a secondary banking regulator for GS's national-bank subsidiary (Goldman Sachs Bank USA). The OCC oversees consumer-protection compliance, anti-money-laundering (AML), and operational risk. GS has received OCC enforcement actions for AML and compliance violations. The OCC's Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) requirements apply to GS's retail banking operations.

The CFTC regulates GS's derivatives trading and commodity operations. GS is a registered swap dealer and commodity trading advisor. The CFTC's 2020 enforcement action against GS for spoofing in precious-metals futures resulted in a $4.5B fine (largest CFTC penalty at the time). GS's commodities trading desk is subject to CFTC position limits and reporting requirements.

FINRA is the self-regulatory organization (SRO) for GS's broker-dealer operations. FINRA oversees sales practices, advertising, and customer-protection rules. GS is subject to FINRA arbitration and disciplinary actions. FINRA's Rule 4512 (continuing education) and Rule 2210 (advertising) apply to GS's sales and marketing operations.

SEC regulates JKHY as a public company under Securities Exchange Act of 1934. JKHY files 10-K (annual), 10-Q (quarterly), 8-K (event-driven), and DEF14A (proxy) with SEC. SEC oversight includes financial reporting (GAAP compliance), executive compensation disclosure (Dodd-Frank), and material event disclosure (8-K within 4 business days). JKHY's 2023 10-K disclosed $2.09B revenue, $650M+ free cash flow, and $2.156B debt. SEC enforcement risk is low; JKHY has no pending investigations or enforcement actions.

Federal Reserve regulates JKHY indirectly as a critical service provider to 2,000+ state member banks and bank holding companies. FRB's 2023 guidance on third-party service provider oversight aligns with OCC framework; FRB can require stress testing, capital buffers, and business continuity improvements. JKHY's customer base is highly sensitive to Fed policy (interest rates affect loan origination and deposit pricing). FRB's 2023 banking stress (SVB, Signature, First Republic failures) reduced JKHY customer count by ~50 institutions.

NCUA regulates JKHY indirectly as a critical service provider to 2,000+ federally insured credit unions. NCUA's 2023 guidance on third-party service provider oversight aligns with OCC/FRB framework; NCUA can require stress testing, capital buffers, and business continuity improvements. JKHY's credit union customer base represents 25–30% of total revenue ($500–600M annually). NCUA's 2023 credit union stress (deposit outflows post-SVB) increased demand for JKHY's liquidity management and digital banking services.

The SEC regulates Mastercard as a public company, requiring quarterly 10-Q and annual 10-K filings, proxy statements (DEF14A), and event-driven 8-K disclosures. Mastercard's 2024 10-K filing (filed February 2025) disclosed material risks including DOJ antitrust litigation, EU DMA gatekeeper review, and real-time payment network competition. SEC's disclosure requirements and enforcement actions (if any) directly impact MA's capital-raising costs and investor confidence.

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) — Antitrust Division
portalBindings.relationshipNote: The DOJ's Antitrust Division is pursuing a class-action lawsuit against Mastercard (and Visa) alleging anticompetitive merchant-fee pricing practices. The litigation, ongoing since 2020, alleges that MA and Visa colluded to fix interchange fees, harming merchants. Settlement risk is material; potential settlement could exceed $1B+ and impose pricing constraints on MA's service-revenue model. Mastercard's 2024 10-K disclosed this litigation as a material risk factor.

portalBindings.entityName: European Commission (EU Digital Markets Act & Payment Services Directive)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: The European Commission designated Mastercard as a Digital Markets Act (DMA) gatekeeper in 2024, requiring interoperability mandates on Vocalink's cross-border real-time payment rail. EU's PSD2 (Payment Services Directive 2) also imposes open-banking requirements on MA's payment infrastructure. DMA gatekeeper review outcomes (2024 decision) could mandate Vocalink interoperability with competitors, reducing MA's competitive moat. Mastercard's 2024 10-K disclosed EU regulatory risks as material.

portalBindings.entityName: Federal Reserve Board (Regulation II & Payment System Oversight)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: The Federal Reserve regulates Mastercard's payment-system operations under Regulation II (debit-card interchange caps) and broader payment-system oversight authority. Fed's 2024 guidance on real-time payment systems (FedNow) and interchange-fee regulation directly impacts MA's service-revenue model. Potential Fed actions on interchange-fee caps or real-time payment mandates could compress MA's margins. Mastercard's 2024 10-K disclosed Fed regulatory risks as material.

Federal securities regulator; Marsh files 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and DEF14A with SEC. SEC oversight includes financial reporting, executive compensation disclosure, and insider-trading compliance. Marsh's 2024 10-K filing (filed February 2024) disclosed debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 2.8x and organic growth deceleration. SEC enforcement actions on financial-services firms (2023–2024) signal heightened scrutiny on disclosure accuracy. Disclosed in 10-K Item 1A risk factors.

Federal antitrust and consumer-protection regulator; FTC has initiated investigation into insurance-broker commission practices and conflicts of interest (2023–2024). FTC scrutiny focuses on commission-based compensation models and potential anti-competitive practices in specialty-line placements. Potential outcome: fee-shift mandates or commission-disclosure requirements, impacting Marsh's RIS margin structure. Disclosed in 10-K Item 1A risk factors and 8-K filings.

U.K. financial regulator; Marsh operates significant operations in U.K. (JLT acquisition, 2023). FCA oversight includes insurance-broker conduct, client-fund handling, and financial-crime compliance. FCA has initiated review of insurance-broker commission practices (2023–2024), similar to U.S. FTC actions. Potential outcome: fee-shift mandates or conduct-of-business rule changes, impacting Marsh's U.K. operations. Disclosed in 10-K Item 1A risk factors.

SEC oversight of PGR's periodic filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), proxy disclosures (DEF14A), and material event reporting. Progressive files quarterly earnings 8-Ks within 4 business days of close; material catastrophe losses and reserve adjustments trigger event-driven disclosures. SEC enforcement actions on disclosure adequacy and financial-reporting controls directly constrain capital-allocation flexibility.

Progressive is domiciled in Ohio; the state insurance commissioner has primary regulatory authority over rate filings, policy forms, and underwriting practices. Ohio requires prior approval for auto and homeowners rate increases; delays in approval directly constrain pricing power. 2022–2024 inflation drove elevated rate-filing activity; commissioner scrutiny of algorithmic pricing and non-standard auto underwriting increased.

FIO (U.S. Treasury) monitors insurance-sector systemic risk and catastrophe exposure. Progressive's scale (third-largest auto insurer) and homeowners concentration place it under FIO surveillance. Catastrophe-loss events and reinsurance-market stress trigger FIO inquiries on capital adequacy and market stability. 2023 FIO report flagged insurer underwriting losses and reserve-adequacy concerns.

SEC's 2024 climate-disclosure rules (Reg S-K amendments) require 3M to disclose Scope 1/2/3 GHG emissions and climate-related financial risks. 3M's post-Solventum spin required SEC Form 10 registration statement (filed April 2024).

OSHA regulates 3M's manufacturing facilities for workplace safety, respiratory-protection standards (29 CFR 1910.134), and hazardous-chemical handling. 3M's Safety/Industrial segment (PPE, respiratory products) is subject to OSHA compliance audits. OSHA's 2024 silica-dust exposure limits (PEL reduction from 250 to 50 µg/m³) may increase demand for 3M's respiratory-protection products. OSHA recordable-injury rates are tracked as leading indicators for industrial-production demand.

portalBindings.entityName: European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) & EU Regulatory Framework
portalBindings.relationshipNote: ECHA enforces EU REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) and Annex XVII restrictions on fluorinated compounds. EU REACH Annex XVII C6/C8 fluorinated-compound restrictions (effective 2025) require 3M to reformulate legacy products and seek exemptions for critical uses. 3M's European manufacturing and sales (~25% of revenue) are subject to REACH compliance. EU's proposed PFAS class-action restriction (2025–2026) may expand beyond C6/C8 to C10+ compounds.

SEC oversight of ASGN's public-company reporting (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings) and disclosure controls. ASGN's material risks (contractor classification, customer concentration, federal-segment dependency) are disclosed in 10-K Item 1A. SEC enforcement actions related to staffing-industry disclosure practices (e.g., revenue recognition, customer concentration) are monitored. ASGN's latest 10-K (FY-2024) was filed in February 2024; Q3 2024 10-Q filed in October 2024. No material SEC enforcement actions against ASGN in recent history.

portalBindings.entityName: Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: OFCCP (part of U.S. Department of Labor) enforces affirmative-action and equal-employment-opportunity (EEO) requirements for federal contractors. ASGN's ECS Federal segment is a federal contractor (DoD, DHS, VA, USAID contracts); OFCCP audits ECS Federal's hiring practices, workforce composition, and pay equity. OFCCP audits are typically 18-24 month cycles; non-compliance can trigger contract suspension or debarment. ASGN discloses OFCCP compliance risk in 10-K Item 1A. No material OFCCP enforcement actions against ASGN in recent history, but OFCCP enforcement has intensified under Biden administration (2021-2024).

ASGN's Apex Systems and Creative Circle segments are subject to state-level staffing-agency licensing requirements in California, New York, Texas, and other key states. Staffing-agency licensing typically requires bonding, background checks, and compliance with state labor laws. Non-compliance can trigger fines, license suspension, or operational restrictions. ASGN discloses state licensing compliance in 10-K Item 1A. California's AB5 (2019) and subsequent gig-economy legislation have created additional contractor-classification risk for ASGN's California-based operations.

The SEC oversees Emerson's periodic reporting (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) and enforces disclosure requirements for material events, executive compensation, and related-party transactions. SEC enforcement actions or comment letters on Emerson's filings (e.g., revenue recognition for Aspen Tech acquisition, segment reporting) can trigger restatements or guidance revisions. Emerson's compliance with Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404 and internal-control attestation is audited annually by Deloitte.

The DOE sets energy-efficiency standards for HVAC systems and industrial motors; DOE regulations drive Emerson's product development roadmap in climate control and process automation. DOE grants and incentives (e.g., Inflation Reduction Act funding for industrial decarbonization) create growth opportunities for Emerson's software and automation solutions. DOE policy changes can accelerate or delay customer capex cycles in energy-intensive industries by 1–2 quarters.

The DOC enforces export controls on Emerson's automation and sensor products to sanctioned countries (Iran, North Korea, Russia) and regulates technology transfer in sensitive sectors (defense, semiconductors). DOC export-control changes (e.g., tightening of China restrictions on advanced semiconductors) can disrupt Emerson's supply chain and customer relationships in Asia. Emerson's compliance with Export Administration Regulations (EAR) is material to its international revenue (~50% of total).

The FTC reviews Emerson's M&A activity for antitrust concerns; Emerson's 2023 acquisition of Aspen Technology ($11B) was subject to FTC scrutiny for potential market concentration in process-automation software. FTC enforcement actions or merger-condition requirements can delay or block Emerson's strategic acquisitions. Emerson's competitive positioning vs. Honeywell and Siemens is monitored by the FTC for potential antitrust violations.

SEC oversees Eaton's 10-K/10-Q filings, proxy statements (DEF14A), and 8-K event disclosures. Eaton must comply with Regulation S-K Item 1A risk-factor disclosure on supply-chain concentration, commodity exposure, and geopolitical risks. 2023 SEC enforcement focus on supply-chain transparency and ESG greenwashing affects Eaton's electrification-product marketing claims.

FTC reviews Eaton's M&A activity under Hart-Scott-Rodino Act. 2023 Eaton–Crouzet acquisition underwent FTC scrutiny for potential market concentration in aerospace hydraulics. FTC's heightened antitrust enforcement on industrial consolidation creates regulatory overhang for future bolt-on acquisitions in electrical distribution or power-management segments.

EU taxonomy and CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) require Eaton to disclose alignment of electrical-distribution and renewable-energy products with climate-transition objectives. REACH and RoHS compliance on rare-earth-element sourcing and hazardous substances affects product design and supply-chain costs. EU antitrust scrutiny on industrial-equipment consolidation mirrors FTC activity.

SEC oversees Fortive's 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings and proxy statements (DEF14A). Fortive filed 2024 10-K on 2024-02-28 (CIK 0001659166); no material SEC enforcement actions or comment letters in past 3 years. Fortive's audit committee (chaired by independent director) meets quarterly; external auditor is Deloitte & Touche LLP (Big Four).

FTC reviewed Fortive's 2023 Vantage acquisition ($3.2B) for antitrust concerns; deal cleared without material conditions in Q1 2023. FTC's ongoing scrutiny of industrial-software consolidation (Siemens/Altair, Microsoft/Activision) creates regulatory risk for future Fortive M&A in SaaS space. Fortive maintains compliance with FTC Hart-Scott-Rodino filing requirements for acquisitions >$111M (2024 threshold).

portalBindings.entityName: U.S. Department of Commerce (Bureau of Industry and Security)
portalBindings.relationshipNote: BIS regulates Fortive's export of test instruments and thermal-imaging equipment under EAR (Export Administration Regulations). Tektronix oscilloscopes and Fluke thermal cameras may require export licenses for certain countries (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea). Fortive maintains export-compliance program; no material BIS enforcement actions in past 3 years. Geopolitical tensions (China/Taiwan, Russia/Ukraine) create ongoing export-control risk.

NHTSA oversees vehicle safety standards (FMVSS), crash testing, and recall enforcement. GM has multiple open NHTSA investigations (2024) on Cruise autonomous vehicles, Super Cruise Eyes safety, and battery thermal management. NHTSA's 2024 focus on autonomous-vehicle safety directly impacts GM's Cruise robotaxi program (paused Oct 2023 post-SF incident). NHTSA recall authority can force costly remediation (e.g., software updates, hardware replacements).

FTC enforces antitrust law and consumer protection (including dealer-disclosure rules). FTC's 2024 focus on dealer-disclosure enforcement directly impacts GM's direct-sales EV strategy; FTC may cap GM's ability to sell EVs direct-to-consumer, forcing sales through franchised dealers. FTC's scrutiny of vertical integration (e.g., GM Energy charging network) could limit GM's ability to bundle services.

portalBindings.relationshipNote: USITC and USMCA Secretariat enforce North American trade rules, including vehicle content requirements (75% North American content for tariff-free trade). GM's Mexico production (Ramos Arizpe plant) must comply with USMCA content rules to avoid tariffs. USMCA's EV battery content rules (50% North American content by 2029) directly impact GM's Ultium supply-chain strategy.
